title: I/O Hardware & Device Controllers
summary: The hardware layer between the CPU and a physical device — controllers, registers, and how the CPU actually talks to hardware without knowing its internals.

slides.markdown:
The CPU never talks to a disk platter, a network cable, or a keyboard's switch matrix directly — it talks to a **device controller**, a small piece of hardware that translates between the CPU's simple read/write commands and the device's messy physical reality.

This group is about everything downstream of that translation: how the CPU addresses a controller, the three strategies (polling, interrupts, DMA) for moving data through it, the driver software that manages it, and the buffering and scheduling that make it all fast. Start here with the hardware layer itself.

slides.sectionTitle: The device controller: hardware between the CPU and the device
slides.markdown:
A **device controller** is the electronics attached to (or built into) a physical device that exposes a standard, CPU-friendly interface — a fixed set of registers and commands — hiding the device's actual complexity. A disk controller, for instance, handles the messy analog reality of spinning platters or flash cells and exposes a clean "read logical block N" interface; the CPU never deals with magnetic domains or NAND voltage levels directly.

This abstraction is what lets one operating system support wildly different disk models from different manufacturers with the same driver code — the controller, not the OS, absorbs the hardware-specific detail.

Every controller exposes a small set of **registers** the CPU can read or write: a **status register** (is the device ready? busy? did an error occur?), a **control register** (tell the device what to do — start, stop, reset, seek), and one or more **data registers** (the actual bytes being transferred, often one register per byte or word, or a small buffer for a block).

A typical interaction: the CPU writes a command to the control register, polls or waits for an interrupt signaling the status register now reads "ready," then reads or writes the data register(s). This tiny register-based protocol is the lowest-level API every OS driver is ultimately built on top of.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: memory-mapped I/O vs port-mapped I/O
slides.markdown:
| | Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) | Port-mapped I/O (PMIO) |
|---|---|---|
| Address space | Shares the regular memory address space — device registers occupy specific memory addresses | Separate, dedicated I/O address space |
| CPU instructions | Ordinary load/store instructions (`mov`, etc.) | Special instructions (`in`/`out` on x86) |
| Compiler/language support | Works naturally with any language that can dereference a pointer | Needs explicit special-instruction support |
| Common on | ARM (no separate I/O instructions at all), most modern x86 devices | x86/x86-64 legacy devices (some still use it alongside MMIO) |

**How to decide:** MMIO has won out almost everywhere because it needs no special instructions and lets ordinary compiled code touch hardware — x86 keeps PMIO mostly for legacy compatibility (some very old device classes) rather than because it's technically superior.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: CPU, bus, controller, device relationship
slides.markdown:
![CPU to controller to physical device chain](assets/cpu-controller-device-chain.svg)

The key separation this diagram makes visible: the CPU-to-controller link speaks a generic, register-based protocol the OS understands directly, while the controller-to-device link speaks whatever proprietary, hardware-specific protocol that device actually needs — SATA commands, NAND flash timing, USB packet framing. The controller is the translator sitting exactly at that boundary.

This is why swapping a hard drive for an SSD behind the same SATA controller often needs no driver change at all — the CPU-facing interface didn't change, only what's on the other side of the controller did.

slides.sectionTitle: How the CPU checks device status: reading a status register
slides.markdown:
Before issuing a command, the CPU typically checks the status register to confirm the device isn't already busy with a previous operation — writing a new command to a busy controller is usually undefined behavior or silently ignored. After issuing a command, the CPU (or, more efficiently, an interrupt handler) checks status again to learn when the operation completed and whether it succeeded.

Status registers commonly use individual bits for distinct conditions — a "busy" bit, a "ready" bit, an "error" bit — so software can test exactly the condition it cares about with a single bitwise AND rather than parsing a whole value. This bit-per-condition layout is why device driver code is full of bitmask constants like `STATUS_READY = 0x01`.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming all I/O uses "special" instructions
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Talking to hardware must require special CPU instructions the OS uses instead of normal memory operations."

**Why it's wrong:** with memory-mapped I/O — the dominant model today — a device register genuinely is just a memory address. A driver reading a network card's status register can literally be a C pointer dereference (`volatile uint32_t status = *reg_addr;`) with no special instruction involved at all. The CPU has no idea, at the instruction level, that this particular load touched hardware instead of RAM.

**Correct model:** the "specialness" of I/O with MMIO lives entirely in the *address* being accessed (a region reserved for a device, set up by the OS and mapped by firmware/BIOS), not in the instruction used to access it. The `volatile` keyword matters here specifically because it stops the compiler from caching or reordering these reads the way it safely would for ordinary memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Real numbers: register access latency vs device operation latency
slides.markdown:
Reading or writing an MMIO register typically costs tens to low hundreds of nanoseconds — comparable to an uncached memory access, since it travels the same system bus, sometimes with extra latency for bus arbitration or PCIe round-trips. That's dramatically faster than the operation the register is describing: a disk seek (milliseconds), a network round-trip (microseconds to milliseconds), or even a flash page program (tens to hundreds of microseconds).

This gap is exactly why polling a status register in a tight loop wastes so much CPU — each poll is cheap, but the CPU can execute millions of them while waiting for one slow device operation, which is precisely the motivation for interrupt-driven I/O, covered in the next topic.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the OS, not the application, owns controller access
slides.markdown:
Device registers are only accessible from kernel mode — an ordinary user-space application cannot directly read or write a disk controller's status register (the [user mode vs kernel mode](user-mode-vs-kernel-mode) protection boundary enforces this). This isn't just convention: it's how the OS guarantees that two processes can't simultaneously scribble conflicting commands into the same controller and corrupt each other's I/O.

Every application-level file or socket operation is really a system call that hands control to kernel code, which is the only code trusted to touch controller registers directly — this indirection is the foundation the entire device-driver model (next topic) is built on.
